summary: A 1976 paper that outlines a high-level framework for sharing resources across a network, rather than only specifying low-level protocols. It suggests programmers call remote services in a uniform way, building on resource sharing as the goal of the ARPANET.

eli5.summary: Instead of every computer needing its own rules, this note suggests one simple, shared way to ask other computers for help.

subtitle: A unified protocol for network resource sharing programs

tldr.problem: Applications wanting to share resources across a network had to build protocol support from scratch, limiting how much they could rely on remote services. The ARPANET's approach required each application to implement its own command-response discipline repeatedly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 707 proposes isolating the common command-response pattern that underlies multiple protocols as a single, reusable application-independent protocol. This reduces duplication and gives programmers a standard runtime environment for network access.
tldr.outcome: The concept influenced later distributed computing systems, though the specific protocol was not widely adopted as specified. The principles led to more modular approaches to inter-process communication.

today: RFC 707 is an early proposal for distributed protocol design. Although not adopted as written, its ideas foreshadowed remote procedure call systems and modern service-oriented architecture.

sections.title: The Case for a Standard Protocol
sections.content:
The ARPANET had grown to support many resource-sharing applications, each with its own protocol for talking to remote services. TELNET let users log into distant computers, and FTP and RJE moved files and jobs around. But every protocol repeated the same pattern: a user process sends commands, a server process sends back responses. Each protocol specified this common command-response dialogue independently, wasting effort and making it hard for application programmers to use remote resources.

This RFC argues that the common command-response pattern should be isolated as a separate, application-independent protocol. A standard protocol would let programmers rely on a single runtime environment rather than reimplementing the network machinery in every program.
sections.eli5: Every computer program that wanted to talk across the network had to build the same basic tools. Why not build those tools once and let all programs use them?

sections.title: The Proposed Protocol Design
sections.content:
The protocol defines two message types: COMMAND and RESPONSE. A command carries a command name, arguments, and an optional transaction identifier. A response echoes the transaction identifier (if present), reports whether the command succeeded or failed, and carries back results. The protocol allows multiple parameters, supports various data types, permits either endpoint to invoke commands in the other, and lets processes suppress responses when not needed.

This design removes limitations of the existing command-response pattern: it supports arbitrary numbers of parameters, handles multiple data types, returns results from commands (not just accept them as input), and allows bidirectional calling. A transmission format encodes these messages for transport between machines.
sections.eli5: Instead of a simple back-and-forth, the new protocol lets you send as much information as you want, go both directions, and skip confirmation messages if you do not need them.

sections.title: Impact and Implementation Strategies
sections.content:
Centralizing the command-response discipline as a separate protocol would let each system build a single runtime environment (RTE) that all application programs could use. Programmers would link a library providing remote procedure call capability into their code, rather than reimplementing protocol machinery themselves. As the RTE is improved, all applications benefit.

The RFC emphasizes that resource sharing works better when programs, not just humans, can invoke remote services. Such a protocol reduces the cost of adapting resources for network use and encourages new resources built expressly for remote access. A request-reply model (an alternative framing) would emphasize the inter-process nature of communication rather than the command-response pattern.
sections.eli5: Programmers could get a standard toolkit to use when they wanted to talk to computers far away. Building new network services would be easier because there would be a common way to reach them.
